name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q01 - Relative speeds and meeting of two moving bodies

questiontext.text:
The position–time (\(x-t\)) graph for two children \(A\) and \(B\) returning from their school \(O\) to their respective homes \(P\) and \(Q\) along a straight path is shown below:

Based on the graph, which of the following statements correctly describes their motion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The position–time (\(x-t\)) graph displays the motion of two children, \(A\) and \(B\), travelling along a straight line from school at position \(x = 0\) (origin \(O\)) to their respective homes at positions \(P\) and \(Q\).
The motion line for child \(A\) starts at the origin \(x = 0\) at time \(t = 0\).
The motion line for child \(B\) starts at \(x = 0\) at a later time \(t > 0\).
The line for child \(B\) has a steeper inclination with the time axis than the line for child \(A\).
The two lines intersect at a single point before child \(A\) reaches home \(P\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The motion is purely rectilinear in one dimension. The position coordinate \(x\) is measured along the straight road from the school towards the homes, taking the direction away from school as positive.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. In a position–time (\(x-t\)) graph, the slope of a straight-line segment represents the speed of the body: \[ v = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = \tan\theta \] A steeper slope corresponds to a greater speed.
2. The intersection of two position–time trajectories indicates that both bodies are located at the exact same position at that specific instant, which constitutes an overtaking event on the road.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Comparing speeds: The straight line for child \(B\) makes a larger angle with the time axis than the line for child \(A\). Therefore, the slope for child \(B\) is greater than the slope for child \(A\), demonstrating that child \(B\) walks faster than child \(A\).
- Comparing departure times: Child \(A\) leaves the school at \(t = 0\), whereas child \(B\) leaves at a positive time instant \(t > 0\). Thus, child \(B\) starts later than child \(A\).
- Overtaking on the road: Because child \(B\) starts behind child \(A\) but travels at a higher constant speed, their trajectories cross at a single point between school and home. Hence, child \(B\) overtakes child \(A\) once on the road.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Child \(B\) walks faster than child \(A\) and overtakes child \(A\) once on the road.

answer.text: Child \(B\) walks faster than child \(A\) and overtakes child \(A\) once on the road.
Child \(A\) walks faster than child \(B\) and overtakes child \(B\) once on the road.
Child \(B\) starts earlier from school than child \(A\) and overtakes child \(A\) twice.
Child \(A\) and child \(B\) walk with equal speed because both graphs are straight lines.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q02 - Physical validity of speed against time graph

questiontext.text:
A student plots the graph shown below for the one-dimensional motion of a particle:

Which of the following statements correctly explains why this graph cannot represent a physically possible motion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The provided graph shows Speed plotted on the vertical axis against time \(t\) on the horizontal axis.
The continuous curve starts in the positive vertical region, crosses the time axis into the lower region below the horizontal axis, and remains below the time axis over a finite interval of time.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The motion takes place in one dimension along a straight line. Time increases monotonically along the horizontal axis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. In kinematics, instantaneous speed is defined as the magnitude of instantaneous velocity: \[ \text{Speed} = |v| = \left|\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right| \] 2. Because speed is the absolute value (magnitude) of a vector quantity, it must always satisfy: \[ \text{Speed} \ge 0 \] Speed can be positive or zero, but it can never take a negative value under any circumstances.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Evaluating the graph: The vertical coordinate corresponds to Speed, with the horizontal axis representing zero speed.
- The portion of the curve located below the horizontal axis corresponds to negative values of speed.
- Since the magnitude of velocity cannot be negative, a negative speed has no physical meaning in real motion.
- Therefore, any graph that portrays a negative speed cannot represent the real physical motion of any object.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Speed is defined as the magnitude of velocity and can never be negative.

answer.text: The acceleration of a particle in one dimension cannot change its direction continuously.
Speed is defined as the magnitude of velocity and can never be negative.
A particle in one-dimensional motion can never reverse its direction of motion.
The total path length covered by the particle must remain constant over time.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q03 - Average speed comparison from position time graph

questiontext.text:
The position–time (\(x-t\)) graph of a particle in one-dimensional motion is shown below. Three equal intervals of time are marked as 1, 2, and 3:

In which interval is the average speed greatest, and what is the sign of the average velocity in interval 3?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The position–time (\(x-t\)) graph shows the one-dimensional motion of a particle.
Three time intervals, marked as 1, 2, and 3, have identical durations: \[ \Delta t_1 = \Delta t_2 = \Delta t_3 = \Delta t \] In interval 1, the curve rises steadily with a positive slope.
In interval 2, the curve passes near a crest where the tangent is almost horizontal.
In interval 3, the curve plunges sharply downward crossing the time axis with a very steep negative slope.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is along a straight line in one dimension. Displacement and velocity directed along the positive \(x\)-axis are positive, while those directed along the negative \(x\)-axis are negative.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Average velocity over a time interval \(\Delta t\) is defined as the change in position divided by the time taken: \[ \bar{v} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{x(t_2) - x(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1} \] Graphically, this corresponds to the slope of the chord connecting the endpoints of the interval.
2. For unidirectional motion within a small interval, average speed is given by: \[ \text{Average speed} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\Delta t} = \frac{|\Delta x|}{\Delta t} = |\bar{v}| \] Hence, the interval with the steepest chord (largest magnitude of slope) has the greatest average speed.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Comparing chord steepness:
In interval 2, the curve is nearly flat near its peak, so \(|\Delta x|\) is smallest and average speed is least.
In interval 1, the curve has a moderate positive slope.
In interval 3, the curve descends very steeply, covering the largest vertical distance \(|\Delta x|\) during the same time interval \(\Delta t\). Thus, the average speed is greatest in interval 3.
- Determining the sign of average velocity in interval 3:
The position at the end of interval 3 is less than the position at the start of interval 3 (\(x_2 < x_1\)).
Therefore: \[ \Delta x = x_2 - x_1 < 0 \] Consequently, the average velocity in interval 3 is negative.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Average speed is greatest in interval 3, and the average velocity in interval 3 is negative.

answer.text: Average speed is greatest in interval 3, and the average velocity in interval 3 is negative.
Average speed is greatest in interval 2, and the average velocity in interval 3 is positive.
Average speed is greatest in interval 1, and the average velocity in interval 3 is negative.
Average speed is greatest in interval 3, and the average velocity in interval 3 is positive.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q04 - Instantaneous acceleration at peaks of speed graph

questiontext.text:
The speed–time graph of a particle moving along a fixed positive direction in a straight line is shown below:

What is the instantaneous acceleration of the particle at the crest point \(B\) and at the trough point \(C\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The motion of the particle is along a fixed positive direction in a straight line.
The speed–time graph shows speed on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis.
Point \(B\) is a local peak (crest) of the curve.
Point \(C\) is a local minimum (trough) of the curve.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Because the direction of motion is constant and fixed along the positive direction, velocity \(v\) is always positive and equals the speed: \[ v(t) = \text{Speed}(t) \] Therefore, the speed–time graph is identical to the velocity–time (\(v-t\)) graph for this motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. The instantaneous acceleration \(a\) is defined as the time derivative of velocity: \[ a = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} \] 2. On a velocity–time (or speed–time along a constant direction) graph, the instantaneous acceleration at any point equals the slope of the tangent to the curve at that point.
3. At any local extremum (maximum or minimum) of a smooth, differentiable curve, the tangent is parallel to the time axis, which means the slope is zero: \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0 \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- At point \(B\): This is a local maximum (turning point in speed from increasing to decreasing). The tangent drawn to the curve at point \(B\) is horizontal, parallel to the time axis. Thus: \[ a_B = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|_B = 0 \] - At point \(C\): This is a local minimum (turning point in speed from decreasing to increasing). The tangent drawn to the curve at point \(C\) is likewise horizontal, parallel to the time axis. Thus: \[ a_C = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|_C = 0 \] Hence, the acceleration is zero at both point \(B\) and point \(C\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Zero at both point \(B\) and point \(C\).

answer.text: Maximum positive at point \(B\) and maximum negative at point \(C\).
Maximum negative at point \(B\) and zero at point \(C\).
Zero at both point \(B\) and point \(C\).
Positive at point \(B\) and negative at point \(C\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q05 - Ratio of distance to displacement from graph

questiontext.text:
A particle moves along a straight line. Its velocity–time (\(v-t\)) graph is shown below:

What is the ratio of the total distance travelled by the particle to the magnitude of its net displacement during the time interval from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 10\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial velocity at \(t = 0\): \(v_0 = +30\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Velocity at time \(t_1 = 6\text{ s}\): \(v(6) = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Final velocity at time \(t_2 = 10\text{ s}\): \(v(10) = -20\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
The velocity changes linearly with time throughout the interval \(t = 0\) to \(t = 10\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is along the \(x\)-axis. Positive velocity indicates motion in the \(+x\) direction, while negative velocity indicates motion in the \(-x\) direction.
The area bounded by the \(v-t\) curve and the time axis represents displacement when treated algebraically, and distance when treated as the sum of absolute areas.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. The displacement \(\Delta x\) is the algebraic sum of the areas enclosed by the \(v-t\) curve and the time axis: \[ \Delta x = \text{Area}_1 - \text{Area}_2 \] 2. The total distance \(d\) travelled is the sum of the absolute magnitudes of these areas: \[ d = |\text{Area}_1| + |\text{Area}_2| \] 3. The area of a triangle is: \[ \text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Calculating \(\text{Area}_1\) (from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 6\text{ s}\)):
Base = \(6 - 0 = 6\text{ s}\)
Height = \(30\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
\[ \text{Area}_1 = \frac{1}{2} \times 6\text{ s} \times 30\text{ m s}^{-1} = 90\text{ m} \] - Calculating \(\text{Area}_2\) (from \(t = 6\text{ s}\) to \(t = 10\text{ s}\)):
Base = \(10 - 6 = 4\text{ s}\)
Magnitude of height = \(|-20\text{ m s}^{-1}| = 20\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
\[ \text{Area}_2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 4\text{ s} \times 20\text{ m s}^{-1} = 40\text{ m} \] - Net displacement: \[ \Delta x = +90\text{ m} - 40\text{ m} = +50\text{ m} \] Magnitude of net displacement: \[ |\Delta x| = 50\text{ m} \] - Total distance travelled: \[ d = 90\text{ m} + 40\text{ m} = 130\text{ m} \] - Ratio of total distance to the magnitude of net displacement: \[ \text{Ratio} = \frac{d}{|\Delta x|} = \frac{130\text{ m}}{50\text{ m}} = \frac{13}{5} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking units and physical limits: Distance must be strictly greater than or equal to displacement magnitude. Here, \(130\text{ m} > 50\text{ m}\), which is consistent with the particle reversing direction at \(t = 6\text{ s}\). The ratio is \(13 : 5\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q06 - Average speed of ball thrown from height

questiontext.text:
A ball is thrown vertically upwards with an initial velocity of \(20\text{ m s}^{-1}\) from the top of a building of height \(25\text{ m}\) above the ground (point \(A\)). The ball rises to its highest point \(B\) and then falls freely to hit the ground at point \(C\), as shown in the schematic diagram below:

Taking \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and neglecting air resistance, what are the average speed and the magnitude of the average velocity of the ball for the entire journey from point \(A\) to point \(C\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial position at roof (point \(A\)): \(y_0 = +25.0\text{ m}\).
Initial velocity at point \(A\): \(v_0 = +20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Final position on ground (point \(C\)): \(y = 0\text{ m}\).
Acceleration due to gravity: \(a = -g = -10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).
Velocity at the highest point (point \(B\)): \(v_B = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Choose the vertical \(y\)-axis pointing upwards with the origin \(y = 0\) at the ground level.
Upward directed quantities are positive; downward directed quantities are negative.
Air resistance is neglected, so acceleration is constant throughout the motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Kinematic equations for uniform acceleration: \[ v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(y - y_0) \] \[ v = v_0 + at \] \[ y - y_0 = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2 \] 2. Average speed and average velocity: \[ \text{Average speed} = \frac{\text{Total path length (distance)}}{\text{Total time interval}} \] \[ |\text{Average velocity}| = \frac{|\text{Net displacement}|}{\text{Total time interval}} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Maximum height rise from launch point \(A\) to highest point \(B\):
Using \(v_B^2 = v_0^2 + 2(-g)(y_B - y_0)\): \[ 0 = (20)^2 + 2(-10)(y_B - y_0) \implies 20(y_B - y_0) = 400 \implies y_B - y_0 = 20\text{ m} \] Thus, maximum height above the ground is: \[ y_B = 25\text{ m} + 20\text{ m} = 45\text{ m} \] - Total distance travelled from point \(A\) to point \(C\):
Upward distance from \(A\) to \(B\) = \(20\text{ m}\).
Downward distance from \(B\) to \(C\) = \(45\text{ m}\).
Total distance = \(20\text{ m} + 45\text{ m} = 65\text{ m}\).
- Total time taken for the motion:
Time of ascent \(t_1\) from \(A\) to \(B\): \[ 0 = v_0 - gt_1 \implies t_1 = \frac{20}{10} = 2\text{ s} \] Time of descent \(t_2\) from \(B\) (free fall from rest at height \(45\text{ m}\)) to ground \(C\): \[ 45 = \frac{1}{2}g t_2^2 = \frac{1}{2}(10) t_2^2 = 5 t_2^2 \implies t_2^2 = 9 \implies t_2 = 3\text{ s} \] Total time of flight: \[ t_{\text{total}} = t_1 + t_2 = 2\text{ s} + 3\text{ s} = 5\text{ s} \] - Calculating Average Speed: \[ \text{Average speed} = \frac{65\text{ m}}{5\text{ s}} = 13\text{ m s}^{-1} \] - Calculating Magnitude of Average Velocity:
Net displacement from launch point \(A\) to ground \(C\): \[ \Delta y = y_C - y_A = 0 - 25\text{ m} = -25\text{ m} \] Magnitude of net displacement: \[ |\Delta y| = 25\text{ m} \] \[ |\text{Average velocity}| = \frac{25\text{ m}}{5\text{ s}} = 5\text{ m s}^{-1} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Average speed is \(13\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and magnitude of average velocity is \(5\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Average speed is strictly greater than the magnitude of average velocity, which correctly reflects the reversal of direction at the peak.

answer.text: Average speed is \(13\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and magnitude of average velocity is \(5\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Average speed is \(5\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and magnitude of average velocity is \(13\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Average speed is \(9\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and magnitude of average velocity is \(5\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Average speed is \(13\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and magnitude of average velocity is \(9\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
